source: NCERT Class VIII, Social and Political Life III, Polity Ch. 7.

sections.heading: 1. What are Public Facilities
points: **Public facilities** = essential services needed by the whole community: **water, electricity, sanitation, public transport, schools, healthcare**.
They are **basic to a decent life** and required in large amounts, so they are usually provided by the **government**.
Access to **safe water** is part of the **Right to Life (Article 21)**, as recognised by the courts.

sections.heading: 2. Why the Government Provides Them
points: Public facilities benefit **many people together** and should reach **everyone equally**, including the poor.
Private companies aim at **profit**, so they may not serve those who cannot pay → the government's role is vital.
The government raises money through **taxes** to provide these facilities.

sections.heading: 3. The Problem of Unequal Access
points: In practice, access is **unequal** — the rich often get better water, power and sanitation than the poor.
Example (water): well-off areas may get regular piped water, while poor areas rely on **tankers or distant taps**.
Some services are being handed to **private companies**, raising the question of **affordability and fairness**.

sections.heading: 4. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Public facilities: water, electricity, sanitation, transport, schools, healthcare.
Basic to a decent life; usually provided by the government (funded by taxes).
Safe water = part of the Right to Life (Article 21).
Private firms seek profit → may exclude the poor → government role essential.
Access is often unequal between rich and poor.

sections.heading: 5. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: Access to **safe drinking water** has been read as part of the **Right to Life (Article 21)**.
Public facilities are meant to reach **everyone equally**, especially the poor.
**Privatisation** of facilities raises concerns about affordability for the poor.
